entry.title: Leetcode - 236. Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
entry.summary:
🧭 Intuition Behind the Recursive Approach
Here’s the deal. We’re going to: Start at the root Ask the left and right subtrees: “Did you find either p or q in there?” If both sides return a non-null result: 🎯 That means we’ve found the split point → this is the LCA. If only one side gives us a non-null: Bubble it up — maybe the LCA is higher up the tree. If neither side finds anything: Return null. We're not tracking paths, not using extra space, and not comparing values — just pure tree structure recursion. class TreeNode { val: number; left: TreeNode | null; right: TreeNode | null;
constructor(val?: number, left?: TreeNode | null, right?: TreeNode | null) { this.val = val ?? 0; this.left = left ?? null; this.right = right ?? null; } }
function lowestCommonAncestor( root: TreeNode | null, p: TreeNode, q: TreeNode ): TreeNode | null { if (root === null || root === p || root === q) return root;
const left = lowestCommonAncestor(root.left, p, q); const right = lowestCommonAncestor(root.right, p, q);
if (left && right) return root; return left ?? right; }
Input Tree: 3 / \ 5 1 / \ / \ 6 2 0 8 / \ 7 4
Let’s find LCA of 5 and 1: From root 3: Left returns 5
Right returns 1
Both sides found a target → ✅ 3 is the LCA.
⏱️ Time and Space Complexity
Metric Value Why?
Time O(N) Must visit each node once
Space
O(H) (stack space)
H = height of tree (recursion stack)
→ Worst case
O(N) (if tree is skewed)
→ Best case
O(log N) (balanced tree)
Don’t confuse lowest with least value
You don’t need to track paths or store parents
Just ask the tree recursively: “Did you find what I’m looking for?” Let the recursive returns bubble up the answer
